title: Rethink data centre planning - Nature Energy
text:
Download PDF

The rapid expansion of data centres is challenging power systems and planning processes to keep pace.

For years, data centres were treated as an unambiguously positive development, as they promised investment, jobs and economic growth. Now the narrative is changing.In July, New York State introduced a moratorium on new data-centre construction, and Texas followed in August by halting new grid-connection approvals for data-centre projects pending a statewide audit. Similar debates are emerging elsewhere in the USA and beyond. In Scotland, there have been calls for a moratorium on new data centres, while Australia is tightening restrictions on data-centre development. These are just a few examples of what seems to be a broader shift in how governments and communities are approaching an industry that, until recently, was largely associated with economic opportunity.What’s driving this shift appears to be a common underlying pressure: data-centre demand has grown faster than the power systems and governance structures needed to support it. In the above-mentioned cases, the governments were responding to a mix of mounting concerns, including the strain on electricity networks, the rising cost of infrastructure upgrades, the implications for water use and land availability, and the fact that many regions still lack clear planning or siting standards for large digital-infrastructure projects.Data centres are unusual electricity customers. Their demand can be enormous because they house vast numbers of power-hungry computers and AI chips, as well as the cooling systems needed to keep them running. The IEA estimates that data centres consumed around 485 TWh of electricity globally in 2025 and projects this to nearly double (950 TWh) by 2030 (slightly more than Japan’s annual electricity consumption today).The challenge goes beyond the sheer amount of electricity involved. Data centres are often geographically concentrated, meaning that even a small number of them can place huge demands on the local grid. They can also be built much faster than the infrastructure needed to serve them, creating a mismatch between the pace of data-centre development and the time needed to expand electricity systems.For system operators and regulators, this creates a difficult planning situation because they must decide which proposed data centres to approve and connect. If they plan on the assumption that every proposal gets approved and built, they may need to invest in grid upgrades to accommodate all the expected demand, only to find that some of the infrastructure is unnecessary or substantially underused later. If they take a more cautious approach, they risk being unable to meet genuine demand when the data centres are eventually built. Conventional planning processes are not designed for such customers.These planning challenges also raise some basic but important questions: who should pay for the new electricity generation, transmission lines, or other upgrades required to connect a data centre? Should the data-centre developer bear the costs entirely, or should some of the costs of wider network upgrades be recovered from other electricity users through, for example, network charges? Virginia recently required data centres to pay upfront for transmission infrastructure built specifically to serve them, a decision that Microsoft is challenging. And when several data centres compete for limited capacity, how should connection priorities be determined? These are not just technical questions. They are very relevant to who benefits from, and who bears the risks of, the infrastructure being built.These questions are already becoming political, as the growing calls for moratoriums and tighter restrictions on data-centre development illustrate. Communities may support investment in new infrastructure when its benefits are widely shared, but that support can be weakened when data centres are seen as just benefiting the companies that operate them. Community concerns about electricity costs and the use of local resources can also make opposition to new developments harder for governments to ignore. Governments therefore need to consider not only whether a data centre can be built and connected, but also whether the wider costs and benefits of doing so are acceptable.This does not, however, mean that data-centre growth should be stopped. Further growth is likely, and the question is really how best to accommodate it. Technology companies like Amazon, Microsoft, and Google have already begun responding to this growth by signing long-term power contracts and exploring nuclear and other low-carbon sources to meet the growing electricity needs of their data centres. By committing to buy electricity over long periods, they can offer power developers greater certainty that the new generation will have a customer. The IEA expects renewables to meet nearly half of the growth in data-centre electricity demand through 2030, with some of this new capacity being financed through power-purchase agreements with big technology companies. Data-centre growth could therefore help accelerate the expansion of clean electricity generation.For researchers, questions must now be asked beyond simply forecasting how much electricity data centres will consume. For example, how can models better capture uncertainty over when and where new data centres will be built, and how quickly their electricity demand will grow? How will this uncertain and geographically concentrated demand affect electricity systems, from grid investment and connection decisions to electricity markets? And how can models better capture the interactions between decisions by data-centre developers, electricity utilities and policymakers? Addressing these questions will require closer integration between research on data-centre development and electricity systems.Data centres are becoming an increasingly important driver of electricity demand, and their rapid growth is putting greater pressure on existing planning processes. How long the current restrictions will remain in place, and what will happen when expansion resumes, look uncertain. But neither continued restrictions nor simply accommodating every new data centre offers a sustainable approach. Instead, data-centre expansion needs to be planned alongside the infrastructure needed to supply it. This means deciding where and when data centres can be built and connected, who should pay for the generation and network investment needed to serve them, and who should bear the costs if proposed developments do not go ahead.
